verdict:
This is a technically accomplished, genuinely intelligent novel that earns most of what it attempts. The central mechanism — a hand-drawn bracket that becomes a ninth numbered line when copied in a coal cellar under bad light, and the "in the morning" that consequently enters a document which originally said "Do not wait for the morning" — is architecturally sound, thematically precise, and arrives with real force. The novel doesn't claim the bracket-to-nine mutation is a metaphor for anything; it presents it as a material fact with consequences that are forensically traced, and that restraint is what gives the climax (Ilinca reading the nine on Strada Crișan's third floor) its devastation. This is not a book imitating literary restraint. It inhabits it.

The three-POV structure holds. Ilinca thinks in columns and nodes and confirmed figures — her accounting metaphors are not applied from outside but generated from inside her job and her self. Munteanu reads documents the way a man who has spent twelve years reading statements reads documents: for where the words diverge, not for what they say. Doina's first-person retrospective voice has the right distance — wry, precise, self-accounting — and is the most formally interesting of the three, particularly in the moments where she addresses an implied reader ("I want that on the record"). The voices are genuinely differentiated, not three instances of the same literary register wearing different hats.

What the authenticity skeptic's eye catches is a different failure: not hollowness but formula. The novel has found its register and plays it for thirty chapters with a very narrow range of emotional modulation. The chapter-ending beats become predictable by chapter 13 or 14: some version of cold/fog/river/lamp-circle/stillness plus a statement of what is not yet known. This is atmosphere as procedure, and it works for the first half of the novel, but by chapter 17 it has settled into a tic that the reader notices rather than feels. The fog is always on the Someș. The lamp is always forty watts. The character is always in their coat. A device that should accumulate has instead calcified.

There is also a concrete inconsistency the copyeditor missed: in chapter 20, Munteanu concludes "He would go to Strada Crișan in the morning," but at this point in the investigation his only address for the G2 node is Dorobanților — given to him by Viorica Damian in chapter 12, noted as unvisited through chapters 16 and 20, and acted on on November 29. The Population Section visit that gives him the Strada Crișan connection doesn't happen until December 1 (chapter 25). The author knew where the chain was going and accidentally wrote the true address into Munteanu's plans before the narrative had established how he got it.

strongest.claim: The bracket/nine mutation is the novel's central achievement: mechanically sound, thematically precise, and arrived at gradually. The difference between a bracket (override, applies at any hour) and a numbered ninth step (sequence item, inherits 'morning' from line eight) is both formally demonstrated and narratively devastating. No line in the novel announces this as symbolic; the symbol works because the mechanism works.

Three POVs are genuinely differentiated and hold their differentiation for thirty chapters. Ilinca's accounting metaphors (nodes, branches, confirmed figures, provisional entries) are generated from inside her professional life, not applied from without. Munteanu reads divergence between copies the way a trained investigator reads statements. Doina's retrospective first-person voice — 'I want to put this on the record' — has the right audience-consciousness and the right distance.

The Munteanu chapters doing textual analysis are impressively credible as period-appropriate forensic work. His reconstruction of the chain through copy divergence — tracking 'by the bed' vs. 'beside the bed,' the long-form vs. short-form line nine, the bracket vs. numbered format — is documentarily sound and never telegraphs its conclusions before earning them.

Doina's wry self-awareness, particularly in the loom scenes and the hostel chapters, is the novel's most formally inventive register. The dry acknowledgment of her own position — the loom noise, the geography book, the bread roll in the evidence drawer — never slides into self-pity or performed stoicism. It reads as inhabited rather than imitated.

The final chapter earns its ending. Doina recites the document from memory on the station steps and her version — with her own copy's variants ('each,' not 'every'; 'Keep and wash,' not 'Wash and keep') faithfully maintained throughout — confirms that the novel has tracked textual variation with complete precision. The bracket she carries in memory is the bracket the novel has argued for across thirty chapters.

weakest.claim: Chapter-ending beats become formulaic by the midpoint. Nearly every chapter closes on some combination of cold/fog/river/lamp-circle/stillness plus a statement of what is not yet known. Chapter 12 closes: 'The afternoon was grey and still, the cold sitting in the valley without moving. He turned toward the main road and walked.' The pattern recurs across Ilinca chapters (lamp on, coat on, sitting still) and Doina chapters (fog on the Someș, walking) with insufficient variation. Atmosphere has calcified into tic.

Concrete inconsistency: in chapter 20, Munteanu ends his day with 'He would go to Strada Crișan in the morning.' But at this point in the investigation, his only address for the numbered branch's G2 source is Dorobanților — provided by Viorica Damian in chapter 12, carried as 'not yet visited' through chapters 16 and 20, and followed up on November 29 (chapters 23, 25). The Population Section visit that connects him to Strada Crișan happens on December 1, in chapter 25. The author knew the true address and wrote it into Munteanu's plans one week before the narrative establishes how he got it.

The full nine-line document is reproduced in chapters 9, 14, 17, 22, 28, and 29. The earlier reproductions serve distinct purposes (Ilinca's master vs. Doina's copy vs. the coal-cellar nine) and are legitimate. By chapter 28, where both N1 and N4 are set down in full, the reader has the text memorized and the reproduction is stalling — marking time while the plot converges rather than advancing understanding.

Minor but verifiable anachronism: chapter 2 states the geography book 'was published in 1978, purchased for me by my mother when I was twelve.' Chapter 19 establishes Doina's year of birth as 1965, meaning she was twelve in 1977 — before the book existed. A child born in 1965 cannot have been twelve when a 1978 publication was available for purchase, unless born in late 1965 (making her barely twelve for only a few months of 1978). The claim is specific enough to be falsifiable.

Doina's narration occasionally over-polishes its retrospective framing. 'The not-knowing was the correct version of not-knowing' (ch. 30) and 'I was nineteen years old and I had the information and I had no instructions for the next step' (ch. 14) are sentences a 19-year-old factory worker from a village near Dej might not produce — even looking back. The retroactive clarity is sometimes too neat, the aphoristic turn too available. The voice is credible for eight chapters out of ten; the other two remind you it is constructed.

quotes.text: That was not an error of copying. That was copying. That was what copying produced, line by line and hand by hand, generation by generation. A word at a time.
quotes.why: The central insight of the novel delivered without fanfare, in the middle of a forensic observation. No surrounding commentary flags it as important. It earns the weight it carries by its precision and by being embedded in Munteanu's genuinely procedural thinking.

quotes.text: An item inside a bracket is not the next entry. It is the instruction that changes what the other entries mean.
quotes.why: This is the thematic core in Ilinca's register — not literary metaphor, but bookkeeping logic. It survives pressure because it describes an actual formal distinction (between a sequence item and a marginal override) that the novel has spent chapters establishing. The sentence is not decorating an idea; it is the idea.

quotes.text: I want to be precise about this: I was genuinely grateful for the loom noise in a way I had not anticipated when I signed my contract.
quotes.why: Doina's wry self-awareness at its best. The sentence doesn't explain or sentimentalize — it simply names a thing that is counterintuitive and leaves the reader to understand why. The formal precision ('I want to be precise') against the absurdity of being grateful for industrial noise is characterization by syntax.

quotes.text: I said: I found it on the bus.
quotes.why: The novel's most important sentence. The surrounding paragraph explains it: 'I did not decide ahead of time to say those words. They arrived already decided.' But the sentence itself requires no explanation. It is a decision, a lie, and a gift — all three simultaneously. Its flatness is what makes it devastating.

quotes.text: The nine is in the left margin. It is in the column with the other numbers, at the same distance from the left edge, the same height. It is not a bracket.
quotes.why: The confirmation of what Ilinca has feared for seventeen days. Three short declarative sentences. The third is the conclusion the whole novel has been building toward, and it lands with zero rhetorical amplification. The 'It is not a bracket' is one of the quietest devastating sentences in the manuscript.

quotes.text: He would go to Strada Crișan in the morning.
quotes.why: Cited as evidence of the novel's central inconsistency: at this point (November 25), Munteanu's only address for the chain's G2 node is Dorobanților. He doesn't connect to Strada Crișan until the Population Section visit on December 1, established in chapter 25. The author wrote the true ultimate address into Munteanu's plans before the narrative warranted it.

quotes.text: The afternoon was grey and still, the cold sitting in the valley without moving. He turned toward the main road and walked.
quotes.why: This specific closing sentence is a marker for the novel's formulaic chapter-ending pattern. Cold + grey + walking home appears in variant form across more than half the novel's thirty chapters. Cited here because it recurs — the rhythm is the same, the fog is always on the Someș — and by chapter 17 or 18 the reader is completing the ending before reaching it.

put_down_points: Chapters 13–15 form a procedural plateau where Munteanu compares copies across consecutive chapters, Ilinca traces branches in parallel, and the scene-level texture is nearly identical across all three chapters (desk, coat, cold, grey). No scene changes register, no new kind of information arrives — only more of the same chain. A reader who is not already committed to the documentary logic might skim or stop here.
who_is_this_for: Readers of literary historical fiction who value procedural precision over pace — the kind of reader who finished Modiano's *Dora Bruder* or Sebald's *Austerlitz* without impatience. Readers specifically interested in women's lives under Ceaușescu's Romania or the bureaucratic texture of Communist surveillance. Not for readers who need psychological interiority, romantic subplot, or scene-level variety. The novel has essentially one register and one key: quiet, methodical, accumulative. If that key doesn't open you in the first three chapters, the next twenty-seven will not either.
